problem: Robotic navigation work (SLAM, semantic SLAM, neural-network agents) treats language either as a command interface or as fixed human-annotated labels and ontologies. It does not use the distributional structure of language as a representational space grounded in perception.
motivation: The symbol interdependency hypothesis says language encodes perceptual and spatial relations, and earlier LSA and transformer studies reconstructed maps (US cities, Middle Earth) from text alone. The author argues that agents could use this to get flexible, data-driven semantics and bidirectional language-perception learning, and could talk about their environment.
key_idea: Treat language as a representational space, not just a command channel, by training agents in a linguistic plus modal 3D environment so that distributional semantics and sensory grounding reinforce each other, as the symbol interdependency hypothesis predicts.
insight: This is a position and review paper with no experiments or ablations, so it offers no empirical insight. Its argument rests on prior work: LSA and transformer embeddings reconstructed maps from text even when the corpus was sparse. It states three untested predictions: language experience helps navigation, language and modal learning reinforce each other, and modal learning alone suffices to produce accurate statements.
method: Survey of SLAM and Semantic SLAM: covers the SLAM pipeline, ontologies, knowledge graphs and semantic maps, and criticizes their reliance on predefined labels and human annotation.
Survey of NN approaches: reviews language as a command interface (imitation learning, meta-RL, inverse RL, PixL2R reward learning) and symbol-grounding work.
Distributional-semantics cognitive maps: reviews LSA and transformer-embedding reconstruction of geographic maps from text corpora.

Proposed architecture (unspecified, unimplemented): an encoder-decoder agent with visual and linguistic processing and 'convergence zones' that integrate the two, in a simulated 3D landmark environment.

Proposed hypothesis tests: (1) pretraining on a corpus describing the environment improves navigation, (2) learning semantics from interaction via an internal monologue helps, (3) exposure to both environments gives more accurate utterances than either alone.

setting.backbone: none implemented; proposed encoder-decoder (transformer-style) agent with visual and language modules
setting.training_data: none (conceptual paper; proposes training on a corpus describing the environment plus interaction in a simulated 3D landmark world)
setting.observation: proposed: visual scene stimuli plus language
setting.action_space: unspecified (landmark-based navigation in a simulated 3D space)

numbers_note: No experiments or results; the paper is a conceptual review and proposal.
results: There are no empirical results. The paper presents a conceptual framework and three testable predictions, and defers implementation to future work.
limitations: No implementation, experiments or quantitative evaluation; the architecture is described only at a high level.
The proposed environment (landmarks in a simulated 3D space) is far from standard room-to-room navigation benchmarks. The survey covers modern VLN and LLM navigation work only thinly.
